And in the year 1440
of the Greeks [1128–1129 AD],
Joscelin entered the territory of Amid,
and plundered the Turkmen and the Kurds who were in Mount Ashuma,
and plundered (and took captive) the villages up to the gate of the city.
And in the year 523
of the Arabs [1129 AD],
when Zengi, the emir of Mosul, heard
that the Sultan wished to give Mosul to Dubays,
he came to Babylon (Baghdad) to the Sultan and humbled himself before him,
and offered one hundred thousand dinars to the Sultan,
and entreated that he would not replace him.
And likewise to the Caliph he offered many gifts,
that he should not permit Dubays ever to rule over any place.
Because of the multitude of wars that took place between the Caliph and this Dubays, king of the Ma'addites (Bedouins),
and how Dubays joined himself to the Sultan,
and made light of the Caliph,
and came to Baghdad,
and began to ride about, and to go in and out without fear (or: boldly),
and to show that he was not afraid of the Caliph.
And a little later, when the Sultan fell ill,
that Dubays stole the young son of the Sultan and fled,
and plundered Kufa, Basra, and Hillah,
and gathered much gold,
and he had with him ten thousand horsemen,
and he took them and entered into the desert.
And the rest of his crafty maneuvers—
since this concise narrative cannot accommodate them—
we have not deemed worthy of recording.
It is related
that in one of the battles that took place between Dubays and the Caliph, Dubays was defeated,
and he alone escaped,
while the rest of his companions fell by the sword.
As he crossed the Euphrates by swimming his horse,
an old Ma'addite woman saw him,
and said to him boldly:
"Dubayr!"
—that is, "unfortunate one!"—
"Have you come?" But he did not become angry,
rather, cheerfully he answered her:
"Dubayr—
that is, the unfortunate one—
is he who does not come back!"
And in this year, the Franks encountered an army of the Ishmaelites (Assassins),
and crushed about ten thousand of them,
and took control also over many of the fortresses that they held in Phoenicia.
And likewise all the Arabs who were in Syria were shaken before the Franks,
and they went and encamped against Damascus and pressed it hard.
And when the Damascenes fixed for them an annual tribute of twenty thousand dinars,
they departed.
